source_text: Et tamen qualem persecutionem patitur frater noster, qui adductus est ad nos? ipsa est persecutio gloriosior; de illa prorsus profiteor. reprehendat qui uult: talem persecutionem profiteor. psalmum lego: detrahentem proximo suo occulte, hunc persequebar. si recte persequor occulte proximo detrahentem, non rectius persequor dei ecclesiam publice blasphemantem, quando dicit non est ipsa\', quando dicit \'nostra est quae in parte est\', quando dicit ilia meretrix est\'? ergo blasphemantem ecclesiam non persequar? persequar plane, quia membrum sum ecclesiae, persequar plane, quia filius sum ecclesiae. ipsius uoce ecclesiae utor, ipsa ecclesia per me dicit in psalmo: persequar inimicos meos et comprehendam illos, et non conuertar donec deficiant. deficiant in malo, proficiant in bonum. fratres, ne putetis aliquid nonum factum esse fratri nostro. pars Donati quando praeualebat Constantinae, laicum nostrum catechumenum natum de parentibus catholicis Petialius tenuit, uim fecit nolenti, scrutatus est fugientem, inuenit latentem, extraxit pauentem, baptizauit trementem, ordinauit nolentem. ecce qualem uiolentiam fecit in nostro! rapuit ille ad mortem: nos non trahimus ad salutem?
thought_title: Persecuting blasphemy as a member of the church
orientation: Augustine is speaking to the congregation about Emeritus, the Donatist bishop present with them, and defending the kind of pressure that brought him there.
pass_a_gloss: And yet what kind of persecution suffers our brother, who has been brought to us? That very persecution [is] more glorious; of that plainly I confess. Let him blame [me] who wants: such a persecution I confess. A psalm I read: [the one] detracting [from] his neighbor secretly, this one I was persecuting. If rightly I persecute secretly [the one] detracting [from] [his] neighbor, [do I] not more rightly persecute the church of God publicly blaspheming, when he says 'it is not [the] same', when he says 'ours is [the one] which is in [the] party', when he says 'that one is [a] whore'? Therefore [the one] blaspheming [the] church shall I not persecute? I shall persecute plainly, because [a] member I am of [the] church, I shall persecute plainly, because [a] son I am of [the] church. Of [the] very voice of [the] church I make use, [the] very church through me says in [the] psalm: I shall persecute my enemies and I shall seize them, and I shall not turn back until they fail. May they fail in evil, may they advance in good. Brothers, do not think anything new to have been done to our brother. [The] party of Donatus when it was prevailing [at] Constantina, our layman [a] catechumen born from catholic parents Petilianus seized, force he did to [him] unwilling, he searched for [him] fleeing, he found [him] hiding, he dragged out [him] trembling, he baptized [him] shaking, he ordained [him] unwilling. Behold what kind of violence he did to our [man]! He snatched [him] to death: do we not draw [him] to salvation?

choices.why: Keeps the comparative force and the paradox Augustine is making: the pressure that brought Emeritus is a glorious kind of persecution.

choices.english: the one who secretly slandered his neighbor
choices.why: Preserves the psalm's wording and the secret/public contrast Augustine builds with the Donatist's public blasphemy.
rejected: the one who backbit his neighbor in secret
the secret slanderer of his neighbor

choices.why: Renders the Donatist claim that the true church is the one in the Donatist party, matching the glossary's 'Donatist party' for pars Donati.

choices.term: deficiant in malo, proficiant in bonum
choices.english: let them fail in evil, let them advance in good
choices.why: Keeps the jussive subjunctive force and the antithesis of failing and advancing.
rejected: may they fail in evil and advance in good
let them be weakened in evil and strengthened in good

choices.term: rapuit ille ad mortem: nos non trahimus ad salutem?
choices.english: Did he seize him to death: do we not draw him to salvation?
choices.why: Preserves the rhetorical question and the contrast between seizing to death and drawing to salvation.
rejected: he snatched him to death; do we not drag him to salvation?
he carried him off to death; are we not drawing him to salvation?

persequar inimicos meos et comprehendam illos, et non conuertar donec deficiant

pass_b_english: And yet what kind of persecution does our brother suffer, the one who has been brought to us? That very persecution is more glorious; I openly confess it. Let anyone who wishes find fault: I confess that kind of persecution. I read in the psalm: 'The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, this one I persecuted' (Psalm 100:5; Psalm 101:5 in Hebrew numbering). If I rightly persecute the one who secretly slanders his neighbor, do I not more rightly persecute the one who publicly blasphemes the Church of God, when he says 'It is not the Church,' when he says 'Ours is the Church that is in the party,' when he says 'That Church is a whore'? So shall I not persecute the one who blasphemes the Church? I shall persecute him plainly, because I am a member of the Church; I shall persecute him plainly, because I am a son of the Church. I use the voice of the Church itself; the Church itself speaks through me in the psalm: 'I shall persecute my enemies and seize them, and I shall not turn back until they fail' (Psalm 17:38; Psalm 18:37 in Hebrew numbering). Let them fail in evil, let them advance in good. Brothers, do not think that something new has been done to our brother. When the Donatist party prevailed at Constantina, Petilianus seized a lay catechumen of ours, born of Catholic parents; he used force on him against his will, searched for him as he fled, found him as he hid, dragged him out as he was terrified, baptized him as he trembled, ordained him against his will. See what violence he did to one of ours! Did he drag him off to death, and do we not draw him to salvation?

problems.quote: dragged him out as he trembled, baptized him as he shook
problems.why: pavens = terrified, not trembling; trementem = trembling. English swaps the senses, losing the contrast between fear and physical shaking.
problems.fix: dragged him out as he was terrified, baptized him as he trembled
problems.ruling: Source: pauentem (terrified/frightened) and trementem (trembling/shaking). English swaps them, losing the deliberate rhetorical contrast in the Latin.

edits.old: dragged him out as he trembled, baptized him as he shook
edits.new: dragged him out as he was terrified, baptized him as he trembled

fixed: Corrected: 'pauentem' means terrified, not trembling, and 'trementem' means trembling, not shaking; the English had swapped the senses.

problems.source_quote: detrahentem proximo suo occulte, hunc persequebar
problems.why: Psalm 101:5 does not match this text; the verse quoted is Psalm 100:5 LXX / 101:5 MT is about a haughty look, not slandering a neighbor. The actual source is Psalm 100:5 LXX (Hebrew 101:5 is different). Augustine quotes the Old Latin from Psalm 100 LXX.

problems.source_quote: persequar inimicos meos et comprehendam illos, et non conuertar donec deficiant
problems.why: Psalm 18:37 does not match this text. The verse quoted is Psalm 17:38 LXX / Hebrew 18:37. Augustine uses the Old Latin from Psalm 17 LXX, not Psalm 18.
problems.ruling: Augustine cites Psalm 17 LXX (Heb 18:37); labeling it 'Psalm 18:37' misleads readers on the scriptural reference.

fixed: The English citation 'Psalm 101:5' misstates the source: the quoted words 'detrahentem proximo suo occulte, hunc persequebar' are from Psalm 100:5 LXX, not Psalm 101:5. Corrected to Psalm 100:5 with Hebrew numbering noted.

The English citation 'Psalm 18:37' misstates the source: the quoted words 'persequar inimicos meos et comprehendam illos, et non conuertar donec deficiant' are from Psalm 17:38 LXX, not Psalm 18:37. Corrected to Psalm 17:38 with Hebrew numbering noted.

problems.quote: Did he seize him to death
problems.why: 'rapuit' means 'snatched' or 'dragged away,' not 'seize.' More importantly, 'ad mortem' means 'to death' in the sense of 'unto death' or 'for death,' but the rhetorical question contrasts Petilianus's violent act with Augustine's peaceful one. The translation obscures that 'rapuit' (snatched/dragged) is violent seizure.
problems.fix: Did he drag him off to death

edits.old: Did he seize him to death, and do we not draw him to salvation?
edits.new: Did he drag him off to death, and do we not draw him to salvation?

fixed: Changed 'Did he seize him to death' to 'Did he drag him off to death': 'rapuit' means 'snatched' or 'dragged away,' and 'ad mortem' means 'to death' in the sense of 'unto death,' so 'drag him off to death' better captures the violent seizure contrasted with Augustine's peaceful drawing to salvation.

dismissed.why: The source quotes Psalm 100:5 (Septuagint/Vulgate numbering), but the Hebrew equivalent is Psalm 101:5, not 100:5. The citation should be Psalm 101:5 with note 'Psalm 100:5 in Septuagint numbering' or similar.
dismissed.note: The site's standard form is LXX 100:5 first with Hebrew 101:5 in the note, so this citation is correct.

dismissed.why: The source quotes Psalm 17:38 (Septuagint), but the Hebrew equivalent is Psalm 18:37, not 17:38. The citation should be Psalm 18:37 with note 'Psalm 17:38 in Septuagint numbering' or similar.
dismissed.note: LXX 17:38 with Hebrew 18:37 follows the site's standard form and is correct.
